pharm: Long-acting, non-sedating selective peripheral H1-receptor antagonist; active metabolite carebastine
tags: Not FDA-approved (marketed in EU, UK, Asia)
quick: 10 mg once daily; up to 20 mg once daily for more severe symptoms
Mild-moderate: no change; severe: max 10 mg/day
Symptom response; ECG if combined with QT-prolonging CYP3A4 inhibitors
summary: Ebastine is a long-acting, non-sedating second-generation H1 antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial) and chronic idiopathic urticaria. It is a prodrug rapidly converted by the liver to the active metabolite carebastine, giving once-daily dosing. It is metabolized via CYP3A4; combination with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole or erythromycin can raise levels and theoretically prolong the QT interval. It is not approved by the US FDA.
indications: Seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis (with or without allergic conjunctivitis)

dosage.d: 10 mg once daily; may increase to 20 mg once daily for more severe symptoms

dosage.c: Chronic idiopathic urticaria (adults and adolescents ≥12 years)
dosage.n: May increase to 20 mg/day per product labeling and response
No experience with doses above 10 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment

dosage.d: No dose adjustment required (mild, moderate or severe)
Per pediatric product (e.g., 5 mg syrup formulations); follow local labeling
dosage.n: Lower-strength/syrup products used for younger children per local approval

admin: Administer orally once daily; may be taken with or without food
Swallow film-coated tablets whole; orodispersible tablets dissolve on the tongue
Avoid concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin) where possible
Do not exceed 10 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment
Continue for the duration of allergen exposure or as directed for urticaria
moa: Ebastine is a long-acting, selective antagonist of peripheral histamine H1 receptors with little affinity for central or muscarinic receptors, accounting for its non-sedating, non-anticholinergic profile. It is rapidly and extensively metabolized in the liver (largely first-pass) to the pharmacologically active acid metabolite carebastine, which mediates the antihistamine effect and provides a long duration of action.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ebastine or any excipient
relative: Severe hepatic impairment (limit dose to 10 mg/day)
Known QT prolongation, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia
Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin)
monitor: ECG/QT when combined with QT-prolonging agents or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors

preg: There are limited data on ebastine use in pregnancy. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; prefer antihistamines with more established pregnancy safety where possible.
lact: It is not known whether ebastine or carebastine is excreted in human milk; use during breastfeeding is not recommended. If treatment is required, weigh the benefit against discontinuing nursing.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in mild, moderate or severe renal impairment. The elimination half-life of the active metabolite carebastine is prolonged to approximately 23 to 26 hours in renal impairment, but standard once-daily dosing remains appropriate.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed in mild to moderate hepatic impairment (carebastine half-life ~27 hours). In severe hepatic impairment there is no experience with doses above 10 mg, so the dose should not exceed 10 mg once daily.

major: Ketoconazole or itraconazole - raise ebastine/carebastine levels and may prolong QT; avoid combination
Erythromycin and other macrolides - raise levels and may prolong QT; avoid combination
Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics) - additive QT risk
moderate: Other strong/moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors - increased ebastine exposure
Rifampicin / CYP3A4 inducers - may reduce efficacy
Drugs causing hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia - increase QT risk
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not clinically affect the activity of the metabolite. No specific grapefruit warning in standard labeling, though grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4.
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction; ebastine does not meaningfully potentiate the CNS effects of alcohol at recommended doses.
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress skin-prick allergy test responses; discontinue several days before testing.

serious: QT prolongation (rare, mainly with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or overdose)
emergency: Syncope or arrhythmia suggesting significant QT prolongation

monitoring: Symptom control of rhinitis or urticaria
ECG/QT interval when used with QT-prolonging drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Serum potassium and magnesium in at-risk patients
counsel: Take once daily; can be taken with or without food
This antihistamine usually does not cause drowsiness, but avoid driving until you know how it affects you
Tell your clinician about antifungals (ketoconazole/itraconazole) or antibiotics (erythromycin) you take
Stop ebastine several days before any allergy skin testing
Tell your clinician if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding
pk: Antihistamine effect within a few hours of dosing
Carebastine peak plasma concentration about 2.6 to 4 hours after dosing
Carebastine elimination half-life approximately 15 to 19 hours (up to ~27 h in hepatic impairment)
Store below 30 C, protected from moisture, per product labeling
pearls: Prodrug rapidly converted by the liver to the active metabolite carebastine, which drives the long-acting antihistamine effect
Non-sedating and non-anticholinergic at recommended doses; flexible 10-20 mg once-daily dosing
QT prolongation is a class concern - avoid with ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin and other QT-prolonging drugs
Cap dose at 10 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment; no dose change needed for renal impairment
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual once-daily schedule - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose data are limited; high doses may cause anticholinergic-type symptoms and, importantly, the potential for QT-interval prolongation. Management is supportive with cardiac (ECG) monitoring, especially for QT prolongation and arrhythmia; gastric decontamination may be considered after recent large ingestion. There is no specific antidote. Contact a poison control center.
